title: Travel
subtitle: journey, trip, voyage, turbulence, jetlag
summary: Talk about travel by road, rail, sea and air, and use the right word for a journey, a trip or a voyage.

lesson.heading: Vehicles and the people who work on them
rows: car, bus, coach, tram, van, lorry
ground staff, cabin crew, air traffic controller
lesson.note: A **chauffeur** is someone paid to drive a car for another person. A **motorist** is simply a person driving a car.

lesson.heading: Parts of a vehicle and the words that go with each kind of travel
rows: petrol station, break down, breakdown service
lesson.note: **Coach** has two meanings: a long-distance bus, and one of the carriages of a train.

lesson.heading: journey and trip

left.label: journey
left.text: A **journey** is the act of getting from one place to another. It is usually longer than a trip.
examples: We had a long **journey** by coach from the north to the south of the country.
Getting from London to the north of Scotland involves a long overnight train **journey**.

right.label: trip
right.text: A **trip** is a short visit somewhere, usually there and back again. We always say **business trip**.
examples: We **took a trip** to the beach last weekend.
She's away on a **business trip** until Friday.
They **went on a trip** to see the Pyramids.

lesson.note: Go on a trip suggests an organised excursion; take a trip or have a trip is something you arrange yourself.

lesson.heading: travel and voyage
lesson.text: **Travel** is a general, uncountable word, used as a noun and as a verb. A **voyage** is a long journey, usually by sea; this use is quite formal, and it also appears in the fixed phrase a **voyage of discovery**.

examples.text: How did you **travel** round Australia? We hitch-hiked.
The liner Titanic sank on its very first **voyage**.
Learning English is a **voyage of discovery**!

lesson.note: Travel is uncountable: we never say a travel.

lesson.heading: Things that go wrong in the air
lesson.text: Elena's flight did not go well: it was **severely delayed**, then **cancelled**, and she was **stuck at** the airport, unable to move on. The airline **put her up** in a hotel (paid for her to stay) and **put her on standby** (promised her a seat if one became free).

examples.text: My flight was severely **delayed** because of bad weather, then it was **cancelled**.
I was **stuck at** the airport all night.
The airline **put me up** in a hotel overnight.
They **put me on standby** for the early morning flight.
The flight left **on time** at 7.00 am.

lesson.heading: In the air and on the ground
lesson.text: **Turbulence** is the strong, sudden movement of a plane in the air; a flight like that is **bumpy**. A **bumpy landing** is not smooth. If the movement makes you feel ill you **get airsick** (formally, you **suffer from airsickness**), and **jetlag** is the tiredness you feel after crossing time zones.

examples.text: There was quite a lot of **turbulence** during the flight, which was scary at times.
The flight was so **bumpy** that I got **airsick**.
We had a **bumpy landing** in Tokyo.
I had terrible **jetlag** for days afterwards.
Soon we were at the **terminal** collecting our baggage.

lesson.heading: At sea
lesson.text: Pieter sailed across the Mediterranean as a **crew member on board** a yacht. When the sea is **rough** it moves violently; the opposite is a **calm** sea. If things go well, everything **runs smoothly**.

examples.text: I volunteered to work as a **crew member on board** a yacht.
Everything **ran** very **smoothly**, even when the sea was **rough**.

examples.note: less formal = I never got seasick

examples.text: I hope the sea is **calm**. I hate **rough** seas.

lesson.text: Say the train arrived **on time** when you mean punctually, not ~~in time~~ - in time means early enough to do something.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence beginning with its ending.

pairs.left: The customs officer stopped the car
pairs.right: and the driver had to open the boot.
and a mechanic came to help them.

pairs.left: The air traffic controllers went on strike

pairs.right: and they had nothing to eat.
and they couldn't get a cabin.
and they had a wonderful cruise.

exercises.prompt: Which words belong to air travel and which to sea travel?
Which words belong to road travel and which to rail travel?
The liner Titanic sank on its very first ___.
exercises.explanation: A voyage is a long journey by sea.

exercises.prompt: How long does the ___ from New York to Rio take?
exercises.explanation: We use flight for a journey by plane.

exercises.prompt: When they were in Cairo they took a ___ to see the Pyramids.
exercises.explanation: A trip is a short visit somewhere and back again.

exercises.prompt: Getting from London to the north of Scotland involves a long overnight train ___.
exercises.explanation: A journey is the act of getting from one place to another.

exercises.prompt: I didn't have a reservation, but they put me on ___ and I got a seat on a later train.
exercises.explanation: Put someone on standby = promise them a seat if one becomes available.

exercises.prompt: The weather was awful and we experienced a lot of ___ during the flight.
exercises.hint: (one word - sudden movements in the air)
exercises.explanation: Turbulence is strong, sudden movement while the plane is in the air.

options: I felt tired for days after flying across several time zones.
My plane sat on the runway for four hours.
I felt ill because the plane was moving so much.
The airline paid for my hotel room.
exercises.explanation: Jetlag is tiredness caused by moving quickly from one time zone to another.

exercises.statement: After we left the airport, we had a long travel by car.
exercises.explanation: After we left the airport, we had a long journey by car. Travel is uncountable, so we never say a travel.

exercises.statement: The train arrived in time and I picked her up at the station.
exercises.explanation: The train arrived on time and I picked her up at the station. On time means punctually.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to describe a good sea crossing.
exercises.answer: Everything ran very smoothly even when the sea was rough.
exercises.explanation: If something runs smoothly, it happens without problems.
